Faculty Senate: Proposal to Support Student Success Context and Background Implementation of Flex-Mix Plan and Student Success The Faculty Senate Officers and Executive Committee have met throughout the fall 2020 semester with different members of the URI community, including student senator Thomas McGrath, to monitor and discuss the implementation of the “Flex-Mix” plan for maximizing safe instructional delivery during the COVID-19 pandemic, paying close attention to student success.
Throughout these discussions, stakeholders from across the community have agreed that, while the fall 2020 semester is indeed challenging in many ways, it is fundamentally different from the aggressive disruption to access to the most basic campus resources and services, and the abrupt pivot to remote instruction that occurred in spring 2020.
In all of these discussions, there has been strong consensus about the power and importance of extensive measures available to both students and faculty to mitigate the challenges that members of our community face.
Our community is and has been demonstrating our unwavering commitment to work for the common good through effective use of these existing measures.

Students from across the university have been exercising their own autonomy, agency and academic responsibility to address and advocate for their evolving needs by: ⎯ Selecting courses based on preferred modality ⎯ Obtaining a laptop computer on loan from URI to maximize success in remote learning ⎯ Adjusting course schedule, course modality and course load according to individual needs and preferences during the add/drop period (or beyond that time via petition) ⎯ Requesting pass/fail option according to individual needs and goals ⎯ Communicating openly with faculty about needs and desires ⎯ Taking full advantage of academic and other support services i.
Academic Enhancement Center (e.g., online learning, stem tutoring) ⎯ Communicating with faculty about unique needs and to request accommodations i.

Disability Services for Students (e.g., information, intake form) ⎯ Strategically using the second grade option (first-year students and transfer students) [UM #8.33.32] ⎯ Requesting grade of “Incomplete,” to complete remaining work at a later date or to re-enroll in the course at the next opportunity [UM #8.53.21] ⎯ Discussing with faculty the option of late withdrawal from a course ⎯ Following normal administrative hierarchy regarding unresolved course-related concerns and problems: faculty, department chairperson, college dean, vice president of academic affairs, and provost. [Student Handbook, pp. 80-81] ⎯ Requesting Ombud services [UM #2.39.10, #2.39.16] Faculty from across the university are exercising the rights and responsibilities associated with their academic freedom to adapt teaching, learning and assessment plans in ways that address students’ needs and demonstrate compassion for students’ unique circumstances: ⎯ Course-wide modifications to assignments, assessments, due dates, etc. ⎯ Use of grading curves and /or adjustment of grading scales ⎯ Provision of extensions on due dates and reasonable accommodations for specific individual students facing unique difficulties ⎯ Authorization of late withdrawal or grade of “Incomplete” to specific individual students facing extraordinary hardships

Faculty Senate: Proposal to Support Student Success The Faculty Senate Executive Committee believes that these existing measures are the most appropriate and effective ways to manage difficulties during this academic year.
Given that current challenges will persist into the future, these measures are the most sustainable strategies, and those that will most effectively prepare our students for long-term success – both during their time at URI and beyond.
Student success and extraordinary measures to alleviate grade pressure At several meetings, the Faculty Senate Executive Committee has carefully considered and discussed the issue of student success and, specifically, whether or not our current circumstances this semester merit extraordinary measures to alleviate grade pressure for students.
Throughout these conversations over the past two months, we have weighed both the benefits and risks associated with different extraordinary measures, as well as the intended and unintended consequences of each measure.
In each case, we have reached the same conclusion: the most effective way to manage challenges during this current academic year is through the existing measures mentioned above.

Meetings during which these matters have been discussed at length: ⎯ September 21, 2020 – Provost DeHayes and Vice Provost Veeger with Senate Chair Echevarría and Senate Vice Chair Cardany ⎯ October 7, 2020 – Faculty Senate Executive Committee ⎯ October 8, 2020 – Senate Chair Echevarría and Senate Vice Chair Cardany with Senator Meyerson ⎯ October 15, 2020 – Thomas McGrath with Senate Chair Echevarría and Senate Vice Chair Cardany ⎯ October 21, 2020 – Faculty Senate Executive Committee ⎯ November 10, 2020 – Provost DeHayes and Vice Provost Veeger with Senate President Echevarría and Vice President Cardany ⎯ November 12, 2020 – Faculty Senate Executive Committee ⎯ November 16, 2020 – Faculty Senate Executive Committee and Senate Standing Committee Chairs ⎯ November 17, 2020 – Faculty Senate Executive Committee and Senate Standing Committee Chairs ⎯ November 18, 2020 – Faculty Senate Executive Committee On Thursday, November 19, 2020, Thomas McGrath, Chair of the Student Senate Academic Affairs Committee forwarded to Senate President Echevarría a Student Senate resolution (passed on November 18, 2020) accompanied by a list of 98 comments retrieved by Student Senate leadership via a student survey.

He requested to speak to the Faculty Senate about the resolution and his peers’ concerns.
At the Faculty Senate meeting on November 19, 2020, Chair McGrath requested that the Faculty Senate consider instituting a measure to alleviate grade pressure for the fall 2020 semester.
During his presentation he noted that he and his Student Senate peers are cognizant of the fact that the challenges associated with this current fall semester are completely different in nature and scale from the difficulties that our community experienced during the spring 2020 semester.
He further acknowledged that he and his peers know that many students do not feel that extraordinary measures are needed, and he underscored that the Student Senate is certain that many students would not take advantage of such measures.

Faculty Senate: Proposal to Support Student Success Extraordinary measure The Faculty Senate acknowledges the Student Senate concerns that, for some students facing truly extraordinary hardships, the extensive measures highlighted above may not be sufficient during our current circumstances.
In response to the Student Senate request, the Faculty Senate Executive Committee recommends that the Faculty Senate approve one extraordinary measure to support student success and alleviate grade pressure, while also minimizing negative impacts on learning and academic excellence.
Expansion of access to the second grade option for all undergraduate students The Faculty Senate Executive Committee views expansion of the second grade option as the most appropriate and sustainable response to the Student Senate request for grade pressure relief.
The second grade option is a measure currently open solely to students who have completed fewer than 30 credits, or transfer students for courses taken during their initial semester at URI.
The proposed measure would expand access to this option to all undergraduate students throughout the entire 2020-2021 academic year.

Motion: In the sole case of the 2020-2021 academic year, temporarily suspend certain parts of section 8.33.32 of the University Manual in order to expand access to the second grade option to all undergraduate students: Amendment to motion to expand second grade option: further expansion of access to graduate students (amendment approved 11/25/20) 8.33.32 Students may exercise a Second Grade Option by repeating a course in which the student earned C-, D+, D, or F.
Only courses that fall within the student’s first 30 credits taken at the University may be selected for this option.
Students must exercise this option no later than the next two semesters for which the student registers after completing thirty credits.
Transfer students may exercise the Second Grade Option for courses taken during their initial semester at the University.
This option must be exercised during the next two semesters for which they register after their initial semester.

When a student exercises the Second Grade Option, only the grade earned when the course is repeated will be used in the calculation of a student’s QPA and only the credits earned for the repeated course will apply toward the graduation requirements.
All grades earned for a given course shall remain on a student’s permanent academic record.
Students who wish to take advantage of this Second Grade Option must obtain approval from their academic deans and submit the appropriate form to the Office of Enrollment Services prior to midterm of the semester in which the course is being repeated.
The Second Grade Option may be used only once per course. (Motion approved 11/25/20) The Executive Committee proposes this extraordinary measure as a sustainable solution to alleviating pressure as different challenges associated with COVID-19 persist and as students adapt to these new circumstances.

Summary description of proposed program (not to exceed 2 pages) We propose an undergraduate interdisciplinary minor in Social Justice & Civic Responsibilities.
The United Nations defines social justice in terms of human rights and personal dignity for everyone.
Other sources include access and equality.
Borrowing from these descriptions, we define social justice broadly as the value of human life, equal access to social capital, personal dignity, and the implementation of human rights for ALL.
US Citizenship and Immigration Services identifies core civic responsibilities that include staying informed about issues affecting your community and participating in them.
More importantly they add respecting the rights, beliefs, and opinions of others, and participating in the democratic process.
We adopt these descriptions of civic responsibilities for the minor.
Course options for the minor represent an array of multidisciplinary and interdisciplinary approaches to social justice topics.
Students who complete the
3 minor will emerge with a nuanced understanding of the world around them, the

4 reasons why people continue to seek to change that world, and a familiarity with the organizing tools and strategies available to those efforts.
A core intellectual component of the minor is an emphasis on seeing the world through the lens of other people's experiences, especially people and groups who have different social, racial, ethnic, economic, religious, gendered, and geographic backgrounds from one's own.
Developing a critical consciousness of the intersections of one's identities, privileges, and power is another important component.
This can lead to more compassionate and meaningful relationships with others.
Moreover, a deep understanding of one's positionality can help perpetuate or dismantle systems and structures that ultimately impact minoritized communities.
Students will learn about subtle and blatant institutional barriers and the micro-aggressions that systematically oppress people.
Students will have experiential learning opportunities that allow them to see the ways in which the ideas they read about and discuss in class actually play out in the real world.

Students will engage in civic processes visiting with community leaders, activists, and politicians to influence policies.
They will prepare for and engage in civic processes reflecting on these experiences.
They will learn theories, methods, and skills that they can use in their work and personal lives to improve the human condition.
Courses for the minor are organized into three categories; peoples, social and institutional contexts, and methods and skills, and students are required to take at least one course from each category (and not more than three) and then complete their credit requirements in consultation with advisors.
An ongoing advisory committee of faculty, staff, and peers will meet once per semester to review advising strategies, and tweak the course offerings, making sure that courses are still being offered, that faculty who teach them are informed about the minor, and review new course options that become available to include in the minor.
The committee will also develop and distribute marketing materials for the minor and maintain a Google work site for students who pursue the minor and for faculty and staff who contribute to it.

This site will also serve to inform the community about experiential learning opportunities that arise in the interest of social justice and civic responsibilities.
Currently, the committee includes several faculty, staff, and undergraduate students.

Why is the new program being developed?
The world is experiencing monumental institutional changes that have arisen from centuries of oppression against groups of people by age, gender, socioeconomic status, ability, sexual orientation, regionalism, religion, race, ethnicity and nationality.
As a species, we cannot tolerate or participate in group oppression any longer, but the institutionalized nature of systemic oppression requires that people must enter the work- force, build their families, and engage in their communities with the knowledge and skills necessary for creating change.
This is the responsibility of our educational system.

Regardless of a student's major course of study, every one of them should graduate being prepared to create positive change that improves the lives of everyone.
A minor in social justice and civic responsibilities, coupled with the student's major course of study provides a path toward creating positive change in the world.
B2.
What is the economic need and workforce data related to the program?
Students who complete the minor will explore their connections to the communities in which they live and work, tackling questions of mutual obligation, social and political change, and human impact on the social, historic, and geographic world.
Grounded in an interdisciplinary approach that includes the humanities, social sciences, the arts, and other fields - this new minor will provide students at URI with a foundation for a life of actively challenging systems of oppression. and decolonizing received wisdom, produced knowledge, and told histories [or public memory].
At the same time, students will gain the critical thinking, reading, writing, and analytical tools that are the foundation of an informed and educated citizenry.

Our students will enter the workforce with skills in human relations that every industry needs for a diverse world.
It is no longer sufficient to train a select few individuals to expertly advise organizations how to navigate diversity.
Everyone must learn the values of a diverse workforce to ensure that each individual can reach their/her/his best potential.
Regardless of a student's major academic and career interests, pursuing the minor in social justice and civic responsibilities will enrich their lives and bring these ideas and skills into all industries, organizations, and occupations.

Since this is a minor and not a major course of study, it is intended to enrich the work and personal lives of everyone, not just those who are in a select few careers.
For example, a student majoring in criminology and criminal justice who pursues a career in policing would be more marketable in that career with a sub-specialty in social justice and civic responsibility, as would a nurse, a teacher, an engineer, or a psychologist, for example.
The skills and information learned in this minor are important for journalists, museum curators, researchers, professors, executive directors of non-profit and social justice organizations, politicians, diplomats, UN officials and advisors, community organizers, community educators (like people at Save the Bay, etc.), entrepreneurs including people piecing together careers through podcasting, and freelance writing.

According to the Rhode Island Department of Labor and Training (RIDLT), the top 10 occupations requiring a Bachelor's degree include registered nurses, elementary and secondary school teachers, and child, family & school social workers.
All of these occupations are projected to show increases in job openings through 2026, all of them require extensive work with the public, so this minor would make our graduates more marketable in these careers.
Organizational rules are changing to include more diverse and equitable processes and roles are being introduced to ensure these processes are followed.
Most people who currently occupy positions of power, in this particular moment, were not taught the skills that are necessary to achieve these goals.
They will be looking for people who have received the kind of education that specifically leads to social justice in any occupation.
A graduate with a minor in this area would be of interest to a company's corporate responsibility division, and human resources positions dedicated to talent diversification.
The RIDLT projects jobs under the Training and Development Specialists category will see a 12.2% increase in jobs by 2026.
